newsitem.title: USA: Zaire woes underscore Africa mineral wealth--Chase.
newsitem.headline: Zaire woes underscore Africa mineral wealth--Chase.

text.p: Civil war in Zaire has shined a torch on Africa's mining potential, but emerging markets must bite the privatization bullet to lure cash for project funding, said Christopher Rocker, group director of global commodity finance at Chase Manhattan.

"I think the challenge for the mining industry is where do you go next for new deposits," Rocker told Reuters. "Africa represents, especially Zaire, Zambia and Zimbabwe, the next frontier for the mining business."
Zaire is in the throes of civil war as rebel leader Laurent Kabila gradually takes over key areas of the country, including the mineral rich Shaba region in the south.

But Kabila's forces took time on Wednesday to sign a $1 billion deal with America Mineral Fields Inc to exploit copper-cobalt tailings at Kolwezi, rehabilitate mines at Kipushi, and build a zinc smelter in Kipushi.

In the past, Zaire produced about half a million tonnes of copper annually, but last year managed only 40,000 tonnes. Cobalt output has also been slashed to about 5,000 tonnes annually, though still a fifth of world output.

"One challenge is for the multilaterals and we, the private sector financiers, to move closer together in our shared objectives," Rocker said. "We probably ought to talk to one another more about how we could be mutually beneficial."
He would like Zaire to step up privatisation and introduce a more stable legal framework.
Zambia is further down the road and, and earlier this week Zambia Consolidated Copper Mines (ZCCM) shortlisted six bidders for final negotiations on sale of its assets.

But financing of projects in Africa will be as challenging for the banks as developing the deposits will be for the mining companies, Rocker said. "There are not many new ways to skin a cat, but there are some new initiatives."
Structured export notes could be one solution.
These were recently used to raise money for Southern Peru Copper Co, the first time in Latin American mining.

The output of a project is sold to a third party outside the country, and the financier discounts the future flow of the proceeds and has, as his recourse, the contract and obligation to make payments to a money center location.

"But to do these things, you need a legal and regulatory framework with some stability," Rocker said. "At some stage in the future, we will see more mining done in Africa, and more financing done in Africa."
Rocker added, "But the mining sector is going to continue to consolidate because it does have a challenge in achieving attractive returns. Prices are volatile and not everything is hedgeable."
Critical mass and size have become important for mining companies when a major project costs about a $1 billion to start up.
Gold and copper still attract most of the money, Rocker pointed out.
